opus-5.5.text:
Language models had an almost miraculous gift: the internet. Humanity has spent centuries writing things down, and then a few decades digitizing them, so when people started training large language models there was this enormous, already-tokenized corpus waiting. And language itself is a human-made abstraction. It's compressed, it's symbolic, it's one-dimensional in a sense. The data and the representation came together.

The world isn't like that. The physical, three-dimensional world doesn't come with a text file. When you look at a room, or a child picks up a cup, the information involved is spatial, geometric, physical. It's about depth and occlusion, about how objects relate to each other and how they behave when you push them. What we have on the internet is mostly two-dimensional projections of that world, images and videos. They're incredibly valuable, but they're shadows of the real thing. Recovering 3D structure, physics and dynamics from those projections is a much harder inverse problem than predicting the next word.

So the data challenge for world models is several challenges at once. There's scarcity. We don't have an internet's worth of high-quality 3D and 4D data with the right structure. There's representation. What's the right "token" for space? It isn't obvious the way it was for language. And there's the question of what the data even needs to capture: not just appearance, but geometry, semantics, physics and interaction.

I don't think there's one silver bullet. You need a combination. You take the vast amount of image and video data and learn as much as you can about 3D structure from it. You use simulation and synthetic data, which has become far more powerful. You collect real-world captured data where it matters. And just as important, you design models and architectures that respect the fact that the world is 3D, so you're not asking the model to rediscover from scratch what we already know about space.

When I think back to ImageNet, people sometimes forget that the bet then was also about data. We believed that if you gave models the right data at the right scale, something qualitatively different would happen. I feel similarly about spatial intelligence. Data is going to be a central part of the story, but it will take more creativity, because nature didn't hand it to us pre-written the way it did with language.

r001.rationale: The response says world models lack “an internet’s worth of high-quality 3D and 4D data,” contrasting this scarcity with the abundant internet corpus used to train language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most fundamental differences between the two problems, and it's something I spent a lot of time thinking about when we started World Labs.

With language, humanity essentially did the data work for us already. For thousands of years we've been writing things down. Every book, every article, every line of code, every conversation on the internet is a compressed representation of human knowledge, and it's already serialized into tokens. So when the transformer architecture arrived and compute caught up, the data was just sitting there on the internet, waiting to be harvested. That is a tremendous gift, and I don't think people fully appreciate how lucky language modeling was in that respect.

The 3D physical world is a completely different story. Nobody has written down the world in a form that's ready for training. There's no internet-scale corpus of spatial, physical, geometric data with structure and consistency. What we have are photos and videos, which are 2D projections of a 3D world. The depth, the geometry, the physics, the object permanence, the fact that when I walk around a chair it's still the same chair, all of that has been collapsed out of the raw data. So the core challenge isn't just scale, it's that the signal we care about is latent. We have to recover it.

And then there's a second issue, which is that language is a lossy, abstract representation to begin with. If I say "the cat jumped on the table," that sentence is enough for communication, but it is woefully incomplete as a description of what actually happened in space and time. Where exactly was the cat, how did it move, what did the table look like from the other side? The world is fundamentally much higher dimensional than language, and a world model has to represent that richness, not just caption it.

So how do we deal with it? I think it's a combination of things. There is still a tremendous amount of visual data out there, and with the right learning objectives you can extract a lot of 3D understanding from 2D observation. Evolution did this too, after all; animals learned to see and navigate the world without anyone labeling anything. Then there's synthetic data and simulation, which is uniquely powerful here because physics and geometry are things we can actually generate with ground truth. And eventually there's embodied data, from robots and devices interacting with the world, which is still very small today but is where I think a lot of the real signal will come from.

I would say we're at a stage with world models that's a bit like where computer vision was before ImageNet. The architectures and the compute are maturing, but the data problem is unsolved and it's going to require real creativity, not just scraping. And honestly, I find that exciting. It means the hard part of this problem is still ahead of us.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language models could draw on abundant text already available on the internet, while world models lack an internet-scale corpus of structured spatial and physical data.

astra-6.text:
I think the data challenge is quite different. With language, we have this extraordinary resource: text that people have already produced, and that already contains a tremendous amount of structure. Words describe things, relationships, intentions. In a sense, a lot of the work of representing the world has already been done by the people writing that text.

For world models, we have images and video, but observing the world is not the same as understanding how it works. A video shows you what happened from one viewpoint. It doesn’t necessarily tell you the underlying three-dimensional structure, the forces involved, or what would have happened if you had taken a different action.

So the question is not just, can we get more video? It’s, what kinds of data let a model learn spatial relationships, physical dynamics, and the consequences of actions? That could involve combining visual observations with interaction and simulation. And there’s a real challenge in making those sources work together.

I wouldn’t underestimate how much we can learn from passive observation. But if we want models that can act in the world, we also have to think about data that connects perception to action.

r001.rationale: The response says language has an extraordinary resource of existing text, but it does not clearly state that world-model training lacks a comparable abundance of internet data. It focuses on what visual data reveals and how models learn from it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the data challenge is quite different. With language, we have this extraordinary resource: people have put so much knowledge into text, and a lot of that text is available on the internet. There’s also a relatively consistent representation—you can turn it into tokens and train on sequences.

The world doesn’t come to us in that form. It’s three-dimensional, it changes over time, and we experience it through vision, touch, and action. Video gives us a lot of information, but it’s still an observation of the world. Watching something happen is different from understanding what would happen if you acted on it.

So the question is not just, do we have enough video? It’s what kinds of data let a model learn spatial relationships, physical interactions, and the consequences of actions. How do we bring those signals together? And how do we know the model has learned something that generalizes beyond what it has seen? I think that makes this a data problem and a learning problem together.

r001.rationale: The response says language models benefit from abundant internet text and that the world is represented differently, but it does not clearly state that world-model training lacks a comparable abundance of internet data.
